blocks.text: 1.2.5 Switch Expressions in Java (Java 14+)
Concept Explanation

Switch expressions, introduced as a standard feature in Java 14, are an enhancement to the traditional switch statement. They provide a more concise and expressive way to write multi-way conditionals, allowing the switch construct to be used as an expression that returns a value.
Key features of switch expressions include:

items: Arrow syntax (`->`) for concise case labels
Multiple case labels per branch
No fall-through between cases with the arrow form (the colon form, `case X:` with `yield`, can still fall through)
Ability to return a value directly
Exhaustiveness checking by the compiler

blocks.text: Key Points to Remember

items: Switch expressions can return a value, unlike traditional switch statements.
The arrow syntax (`->`) allows for more concise case definitions.
Multiple case labels can be combined using commas.
There's no fall-through between cases when using the arrow syntax.
The `yield` keyword is used to return a value from a block in a switch expression.
Switch expressions must be exhaustive (cover all possible cases).

blocks.text: Java 14+ Features

items: Introduction of the `->` syntax for concise case labels
Ability to use switch as an expression
Multiple case labels per branch
The `yield` keyword for returning values from blocks

blocks.text: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

items: Forgetting to cover all possible cases: Ensure all possible values are handled or include a default case.
Mistakenly allowing fall-through: When using the arrow syntax, fall-through doesn't occur automatically.
Forgetting to use `yield` in block cases: Use `yield` to return a value from a multi-statement case block.

blocks.text: Best Practices and Optimization Techniques

items: Use switch expressions for concise, value-returning switches.
Combine case labels when the same action applies to multiple values.
Prefer the arrow syntax for single-expression cases.
Use blocks with `yield` for complex case logic.
Leverage pattern matching in switch (standard since Java 21, JEP 441) for more powerful switches.

blocks.text: Edge Cases and Their Handling

items: Null values: Without a `case null` label, a switch throws `NullPointerException` on null. Since Java 21 you can add `case null ->`; otherwise use a preceding null check.
Enum switches: Ensure all enum constants are covered or include a default case.
Exhaustiveness with sealed classes: When switching on sealed classes, cover all permitted subclasses.

blocks.text: Interview-specific Insights

items: Be prepared to compare switch expressions with traditional switch statements.
Understand the benefits of switch expressions in terms of readability and safety.
Know how to refactor a traditional switch statement into a switch expression.
Be aware of the latest developments, such as pattern matching in switch (standard since Java 21).

blocks.text: Interview Q&A
Q1: What are the main advantages of switch expressions over traditional switch statements?
A1: Switch expressions offer several advantages:

items: Conciseness: They allow for more compact code, especially with the arrow syntax.
Safety: They eliminate accidental fall-through between cases.
Expressiveness: They can be used as expressions, returning values directly.
Exhaustiveness: The compiler checks if all possible cases are covered.
Multiple case labels: You can combine multiple case labels in a single branch.

A3: The compiler performs exhaustiveness checking for switch expressions, ensuring that all possible values of the switched variable are handled.
